messages.author: b78114f8e8a68ea3
messages.subject: PLS.Pooled.within
parts:
Dear community,

I would like to perform an integration.test using two 3 D data matrices of 20 and 30 landmarks respectively.

The thing is that I would like to remove the variation related to population and sex previous to analyze integration. To do so I’ve calculated the pooled-within vcv matrices using the cov.W function (Le Maitre and Mitteroecker, in press).

The problem is that I cannot use them to perform a PLS because they have a different number of dimensions due to the different number of landmarks. However, if they had, that would not be possible to plot them because there is not information about the individuals but the VCVs.

My question is: is there a way to perform a two.b.pls/integration.test analysis taking into account the within group variation?

Thanks in advance,

E.

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] PLS.Pooled.within
parts:
Eric,

I feel you are missing an important connection for what the pooled within-group VCV is and how it is calculated.  If one has a linear model, e.g., lm(Y ~ group), from which they obtain residuals (R), then W = crossprod(R) / df, where df is the appropriate residual degrees of freedom.  (Note: the cov.W function in the vcvComp package calculates an unweighted mean of single-group covariance matrices, irrespective of the number of observations per group, meaning small groups and large groups contribute equally to the estimate of the pooled within-group covariance matrix.  This is not consistent with the cov function in R and not something I feel is appropriate.  The two functions will produce similar covariance matrices if and only if data are balanced.  You have been warned!)

It’s the residuals that are values independent of the effect of groups, like population:sex levels.  Using such residuals in a PLS analysis should accomplish what you seek to accomplish.

If this explanation does not make sense (to anyone reading this), my first recommendation would be to become comfortable with what linear models are , what they do, and how they can be used.  Trying to understand what a residual (e.g., pooled within-group) covariance matrix is and does without understanding the linear algebra of linear models will always have limited utility.  

Good luck!
Mike
